name: AP Calculus AB
overview: AP Calculus AB is the equivalent of a first-semester college calculus course: limits and continuity, derivatives and their applications, integrals and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, separable differential equations, and applications of integration (area, volume, accumulation, average value, motion). The exam rewards fluent procedures, moving between graphs, tables, formulas, and words, and written calculus justifications.
examMode: Hybrid digital: multiple-choice answered in Bluebook; free-response questions viewed in Bluebook and handwritten in a paper booklet.

sections.name: Section I, Part A
sections.notes: New for May 2027: 29 questions in 62 minutes (was 30 in 60).

sections.name: Section I, Part B
sections.notes: New for May 2027: 13 questions in 38 minutes (was 15 in 45). Only some items actually need the calculator.

sections.name: Section II, Part B
sections.notes: At least 2 of the 6 FRQs use a real-world context.

units.title: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

skills.name: 1. Implementing Mathematical Processes
skills.description: Determine expressions and values using mathematical procedures and rules (limits, derivatives, antiderivatives, Riemann sums, series tests). About 50–70% of MCQ and 35–60% of FRQ points (AB weights; BC similar).

skills.name: 2. Connecting Representations
skills.description: Translate mathematical information within or across representations: graphs, tables, formulas, and verbal descriptions. About 15–30% of MCQ and 10–20% of FRQ.

skills.name: 3. Justification
skills.description: Justify reasoning and solutions: verify theorem hypotheses (IVT, MVT, EVT), justify extrema, concavity, and convergence with calculus-based reasons. About 10–20% of MCQ and 35–60% of FRQ — the biggest FRQ point source.

skills.name: 4. Communication and Notation
skills.description: Use correct notation, units, and language in context (free-response only, about 10–25%): write limits, integrals, and derivatives correctly, and interpret answers with units.

scoring.summary: Section I (42 MCQ) and Section II (6 FRQs × 9 points = 54 points) each count 50%. Raw scores are weighted into a composite, and College Board converts the composite to a 1–5 score using cut points that vary by year and are not published.

frqTypes.name: Rates/accumulation in context (often with a table)
frqTypes.howScored: Points for setting up integrals of rates, Riemann/trapezoidal estimates with correct units, interpreting values in context, and using the FTC (amount = initial + ∫ rate). Calculator questions reward the setup plus a 3-decimal answer.

frqTypes.name: Particle motion / position–velocity–acceleration
frqTypes.howScored: Points for v = x′, a = v′, speeding up/slowing down via the signs of v and a, total distance with |v|, and position from initial position plus net change.

frqTypes.name: Graph of f′ (or of f) analysis
frqTypes.howScored: Points for locating extrema/inflection points WITH a correct reason referencing f′ or f″ sign changes, evaluating accumulation functions with geometry, and Candidates-Test extreme values.

frqTypes.name: Differential equations
frqTypes.howScored: Typical split: slope field sketch (1), tangent-line approximation (2), separation of variables (5: separate, antiderivatives, constant, use initial condition, solve for y). Solutions without separation earn no credit on the separation part.

frqTypes.name: Area and volume
frqTypes.howScored: Points for correct integrand and limits (often an integrand point and a limits/constant point), and an answer; cross-section and washer setups are scored separately from the evaluation.

frqTypes.name: Function analysis / implicit differentiation / tables
frqTypes.howScored: Points for applying theorems (MVT/IVT) with hypotheses stated, implicit derivatives, tangent lines, and limits (including L’Hospital’s Rule with verification of the indeterminate form).

strategy: Part A MCQ (no calculator) is 29 questions in 62 minutes — just over 2 minutes each. Do the quick derivative/limit items first and flag long ones.

Part B MCQ (13 questions, 38 minutes) and FRQ Part A require a graphing calculator: know how to graph, find zeros/intersections, numerically differentiate (nDeriv) and integrate (fnInt), and STORE intermediate values instead of retyping rounded ones.
Report decimal answers correct to three places after the decimal point; rounding early (e.g., storing a bound as 2.3 instead of 2.30259…) is a classic lost point.
On FRQs, write the setup (the integral or derivative expression) before the number. A bare calculator answer often earns no credit; the setup point is frequently separate from the answer point.
Justifications must name the calculus reason: “f′ changes from positive to negative at x = 3, so f has a relative maximum there,” not “the graph goes up then down.”
When a theorem is used (IVT, MVT, EVT), explicitly state that its hypotheses (continuity, differentiability) are met, citing the given information.
Answer in context with units: “the rate at which water is leaving the tank is 4.2 gallons per hour at t = 3.”
Never leave an FRQ part blank: parts are scored independently, and a correct setup or a correct use of an earlier (even wrong) answer can still earn points.
pitfalls: Confusing f, f′, and f″ when reading a graph of f′ — e.g., treating the maximum of f′ as the maximum of f.
Dropping the inner derivative in the chain rule, especially with trig, exponential, and inverse functions.
Writing equations that are false, such as linking unequal expressions with “=” (e.g., ‘f′(x) = 3x² = 12’). Readers penalize false statements.
Using a sign chart of f instead of f′ (or f″) to justify extrema or inflection points.
Forgetting that ∫ₐᵇ r(t) dt is net change, not total distance; total distance needs |v|.
Omitting the constant of integration, or failing to use the initial condition to solve for C, in separable differential equations.
Rounding intermediate calculator results and getting a final answer off in the third decimal place.
referenceSheet: None. No formula sheet is provided on AP Calculus AB; all derivative/integral rules, geometry formulas, and theorems must be memorized.

caveats: May 2027 MCQ format changed: Part A is 29 questions/62 minutes and Part B is 13 questions/38 minutes (previously 30/60 and 15/45). Course content did not change.
The 35%/15% split between MCQ Parts A and B is as listed on the AP Students page for 2027; older materials list 33.3%/16.7%.
Approximate cutoffs are estimates based on historical released-exam conversions (older format); College Board does not publish cut scores and they vary year to year.
The CED's own Exam Information section uses slightly different unit names in one table (e.g., 'Applying Derivatives to Analyze Functions'); the official framework titles are used here.
